items.p: What is a property of a material?
opts: A word that tells what the material is like
The name of the object it makes
The shop where it is sold
items.why: A property is a word like hard, shiny or waterproof. It tells what the material is like. Picking 'the name of the object' mixes up object and material. A spoon is an object. Steel is the material. Picking 'how much it costs' is about price, which is not what the material is like.
items.art: A steel spoon with three labels: hard, shiny, heavy.

items.p: A steel tumbler and a steel spoon are two different objects. What is the same about them?
items.why: Both are made of steel. The material is the same, so its properties, like hard and shiny, are the same. Picking shape, size or use mixes up the object and the material. Objects can have different shapes and uses even when the material is the same.

items.p: Sort these into hard and soft. Hard means hard to scratch.
items.a: see items
items.why: A nail, granite and glass are hard to scratch. Chalk, soap and wax are easy to scratch with a fingernail. People also call cotton wool soft, but that is a different meaning of soft, which is squashy. In science, hard and soft are about scratching.

items.p: A material that lets no light through is ____.
items.why: Opaque means no light comes through. Transparent lets light through clearly. Translucent lets light through, but blurred.

items.p: Match each property to a simple test.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each property has a test that shows it. Hard is about scratching. Flexible is about bending. Waterproof is about water staying out. Transparent is about seeing through. Strong is about how much weight it holds before breaking.

items.p: In a room, a steel spoon is colder than a wooden spoon.
items.why: False. Both are the same temperature as the room. The steel spoon only feels colder, because it carries heat away from your hand faster. A thermometer would show the same number for both.

items.p: Which property makes a cotton towel good for drying you?
items.why: Absorbent means it soaks up water into its tiny gaps. Picking waterproof is the opposite, because a waterproof towel would push the water around on your skin. Picking shiny or rigid has nothing to do with drying.

items.p: Put these in order from MOST flexible to LEAST flexible. A cotton cloth, a sheet of paper, a thin cardboard, a wooden stick.
items.a: order shown
items.why: Cloth bends in any direction with the lightest touch. Paper bends easily but holds a fold. Cardboard is stiffer. The wooden stick hardly bends at all. This is an example of comparing materials in a ladder from most to least.

items.p: A glass tumbler is hard to scratch, but it breaks when dropped. What does this tell you?
opts: Glass is hard and also brittle
items.why: Hard is about scratching. Brittle is about snapping or shattering. Glass is both hard and brittle. Picking 'glass is strong' mixes up hard and strong. Many people think hard means unbreakable, but a hard thing can still shatter.

items.p: One sheet of butter paper and a tall stack of butter paper let through the same amount of light.
items.why: False. One sheet lets a lot of light through. A tall stack lets almost none. So a material's property can change with its thickness.
items.context: Butter paper is thin, greaseproof paper used in kitchens. Light passes through it, but blurred.

items.p: You want to compare how strong a paper strip and a cloth strip are. What is the fairest way?
opts: Cut both the same width and length, and pour water one cup at a time into a bag hanging from each
Pull the paper hard and the cloth gently
Use a wide paper strip and a thin cloth strip
Look at which one seems stronger
items.why: To compare fairly, change only the material. Keep the width, length and method the same. Picking different widths changes more than one thing. Picking 'looks stronger' is a guess, not a test.
items.context: In the dry or damp test, you hang a bag from a strip. You pour in water, one cup at a time, until the strip tears.

items.p: A material that snaps or shatters instead of bending is called ____.
items.why: Brittle things, like glass bangles, dry biscuits and chalk, break into pieces when pushed too far. They do not bend first.

items.p: Choose one object at home. Write four properties of its material. For each one, say how you found out.
items.a: Any object with four right properties and a way to test each. For example, a steel tumbler. It is shiny, because I can see my face in it. It is hard, because my fingernail cannot scratch it. It is waterproof, because water stays inside. It rings when I tap it with a spoon.
items.why: Each property should come with a way of finding it out, by looking, touching, listening or testing.

items.p: In the dry or damp test, a newspaper strip held 6 cups of water when dry and 1 cup when damp. What can you say?
opts: The damp strip held 5 cups less, so water made it much weaker
Dry and damp paper are the same
You cannot say anything from numbers
items.why: 6 take away 1 is 5. So the damp strip held 5 cups less than the dry one. Water gets between the paper fibres and loosens the joins that hold them together. Picking 'stronger' usually means thinking that wet things must be tougher because they feel heavy.
items.context: In the dry or damp test, you hang a bag from a strip and pour in water, one cup at a time, until the strip tears. You do it once with a dry strip and once with a damp strip.

items.p: The handle of a tawa or a frying pan is often made of wood or plastic. Why not steel?
items.a: Steel carries heat very well, so a steel handle would get too hot to hold. Wood and plastic carry heat slowly. They are insulators. So the handle stays cool enough to hold.
items.why: Steel is a conductor of heat and wood or plastic is an insulator. The pan needs the first and the handle needs the second.

items.p: Draw a ladder with four rungs. Put four things on it, from the hardest at the top to the softest at the bottom.
items.a: Any four things in a sensible order. For example, from top to bottom: diamond, steel nail, fingernail, chalk.
items.why: A ladder puts things in order. A child can check each step: does the upper one scratch the lower one?
items.art: A blank ladder with four rungs and space to draw.

items.p: Chalk scratches soap. A fingernail scratches chalk. A steel nail scratches a fingernail. Put them in order from SOFTEST to HARDEST: steel nail, soap, fingernail, chalk.
items.a: order shown
items.why: If A scratches B, then A is harder than B. So soap is below chalk, chalk is below the fingernail and the fingernail is below the nail. Putting several things in order from clues is how Friedrich Mohs built his ladder of hardness.

items.p: A steel nail scratches a piece of copper. A fingernail cannot. What does this tell you about the copper?
opts: It is harder than a fingernail, and softer than the nail
It is softer than a fingernail
It is harder than the nail
Nothing, because scratching tells us nothing
items.why: The nail scratched the copper, so the copper is softer than the nail. The fingernail could not scratch the copper, so the copper is harder than the fingernail. That places it between the two. Picking 'softer than a fingernail' reverses the clue.
items.context: This is about the scratch test. If one thing scratches another, the first is harder.

items.p: A steel ship floats, but a steel nail sinks. Why?
opts: The ship is hollow, so on average it is less packed than water
The ship is lighter than the nail
The sea pushes harder on big things
Ships are made of a special steel
items.why: A ship has a huge space inside, full of air. Counting steel and air together, a ship is less packed than the water it pushes aside, so it floats. A nail is solid steel, which is more packed than water. Picking 'lighter' is the common mistake. A ship weighs thousands of tonnes.

items.p: A diamond and the black lead of a pencil are made of the same kind of atom.
items.why: True. Both are only carbon. The difference is how the atoms are joined. In diamond they are locked in all directions. In graphite they lie in sheets that slide.

items.p: A steel plate and a plastic plate come out of the same freezer. The steel plate feels colder. Why?
opts: Steel carries heat out of your hand faster
Plastic is warmer in the middle
items.why: Both plates are at the same temperature. Steel is a conductor, so it pulls heat out of your fingers quickly, and your skin feels that as cold. Plastic is an insulator, so heat leaves your hand slowly. Picking 'steel holds more cold' is the common idea that cold is something stored inside things.

items.p: Water climbing up through the tiny gaps in a paper towel is called ____.
items.why: Wicking is water creeping up through tiny gaps, even upwards against gravity. It is how a diya wick lifts oil and how a towel soaks up a spill.

items.p: In the story, cotton thread held 14 shells in the damp dawn and only 11 at dry noon. What is the best explanation?
opts: Cotton thread is stronger when it is damp
The shells were heavier at noon
The cotton changed into another material
items.why: Shefali used the same thread, the same length and the same shells. Only the dampness of the air changed. Then she made a noon thread damp, and it held 14. So damp makes cotton a little stronger. Picking 'tired' does not fit the test, because a damp thread at noon held as much as a dawn thread.
items.context: In the story The Thread That Held at Dawn, a girl called Shefali hung threads from a pole. She added white cowrie shells one by one until each thread snapped.

items.p: Match each material to what is happening inside it.
pairs: Each atom is locked to four neighbours
Atoms lie in flat sheets that slide
Some electrons roam between the atoms
Long tangled chains that straighten when pulled
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These pictures explain properties. Locked atoms make diamond hard. Sliding sheets make graphite soft. Roaming electrons make metals shiny and good at carrying heat. Tangled chains make rubber stretchy.

items.p: Sort these into conductors and insulators of heat.
items.a: see items
items.why: Metals carry heat quickly. Wood, wool and plastic carry it slowly. A woollen shawl keeps you warm because it traps air, and air is a poor conductor. It does not make heat.

items.p: You want to know whether a rubber band or a thread stretches more. Which is the fairest test?
opts: Start both at the same length and hang the same weight. Measure the stretch in centimetres
Pull the thread harder than the rubber band
Start with a long thread and a short rubber band
Pull both and see which feels stretchier
items.why: A fair test changes only the material. The starting length and the weight must be the same, and the stretch measured with a ruler. Picking different lengths or pulls changes more than one thing.
items.context: Stretchy means it gets longer when pulled, and springs back when you let go.

items.p: On the Mohs scale, diamond at 10 is exactly 10 times as hard as talc at 1.
items.why: False. The numbers only give the order. Diamond is far harder than the next mineral, corundum at 9, not just a little harder. A ladder tells you who is above whom, not by how much.

items.p: Look at the table. Which material is the most rigid?

chart.title: Made-up example: how far each strip drooped over the table edge

items.why: In the droop test, the more rigid a strip is, the less its end droops. The corrugated card drooped just 1 centimetre, the least. Picking cloth is the common mistake of reading a big number as 'more'. Here a big droop means more flexible, not more rigid.
items.context: In the droop test, you push a strip over a table edge. You measure how far its tip bends down.

items.p: A strip held 6, 5 and 6 cups of water in three tries. Another strip held 2, 7 and 4. Which result can you trust more?
opts: The first, because the three numbers are close
Neither, because tests are never reliable
items.why: When repeated tries give close numbers, the result is reliable. When they are far apart, something changed between tries, such as the method. Picking the second because of the biggest number would be trusting the luckiest try.
items.context: In the dry or damp test, you hang a bag from a strip and pour in water until the strip tears. You repeat the test to see whether the results are reliable.

items.p: Name one property that matters most for school shoes, and one for a school bag. Explain your choices.
items.a: For shoes, grip or strong and flexible, because shoes must bend with the foot and not slip. For a bag, strong and waterproof, because it holds heavy books and must survive rain. Any sensible choice with a reason is right.
items.why: The job decides which property matters. A good answer says what the object must do, then names the property that does it.

items.p: Draw a torch beam meeting three materials: clear glass, butter paper and a steel plate. Show what the light does in each.
items.a: Clear glass: the beam goes straight through. Butter paper: the beam goes in but spreads out in all directions. Steel plate: the beam stops or bounces back.
items.why: Transparent materials let the light pass straight. Translucent ones scatter it. Opaque ones soak it up or bounce it back.
items.art: Three blank boxes, each with a torch on the left.

items.p: Look at the table. Which surface is the most absorbent?

chart.title: Made-up example: seconds for one drop to vanish

items.why: The drop vanished fastest on the paper towel, in 2 seconds, so it is the most absorbent. Picking the plastic bag mixes up a long time with a good result. A long time means the water stayed on top, which means waterproof.
items.context: In the vanishing drop test, you put one drop of water on each surface. You time how long it takes to vanish.

items.p: It is easy to measure how long a rope is. Why is it harder to measure how hard a stone is?
items.a: Length has one clear way to measure it, with a ruler. 'Hard' could mean hard to scratch, hard to dent or hard to break, and these tests give different orders. So scientists use several hardness scales.
items.why: Hardness is really a family of properties. Scientists must say which test they used before they give a number.

items.p: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon. What makes diamond hard and graphite soft?
opts: How the carbon atoms are joined
Graphite is made of a different atom
items.why: In diamond every atom is locked to four others in all directions. In graphite the atoms lie in flat sheets that slide over each other. Picking 'different atom' is a natural guess, because they look so unlike. But they are the same atom. The pattern is the difference.

items.p: Why do metals feel cold and look shiny?
opts: Some of their electrons roam freely, carrying heat and bouncing light
Metals are always colder than other things
Metals have no atoms in them
items.why: In a metal, some electrons are not tied to one atom. They carry heat away from your hand quickly, so metal feels cold. They also bounce light back, which makes metals shiny. Picking 'always colder' is the idea this unit tested and rejected.

items.p: Invent a test for a property we have not tested, such as how sticky a tape is. Say what you would measure, what you would keep the same, and the unit.
items.a: For stickiness: stick the same length of tape to the same smooth table. Hang a small bag from the free end. Pour in water one spoon at a time until the tape peels off. Keep the tape length, the table and the way I press it the same. The unit is spoons of water.
items.why: A good test measures one thing, keeps everything else the same, and gives a number with a unit. This is what the testing-materials unit is all about.

items.p: Which property matters most for each job?
items: A rope for lifting a bucket from a well
A cloth for wiping a spill
items.a: see items
items.why: The job decides the property. The window must let you see out. The rope must not snap. The cloth must soak up water. The tea cosy must keep heat in. The band must stretch and spring back.
items.context: This question links jobs to properties. A property matters because a job needs it.

items.p: What happens to each material when it gets damp?
items.a: see items
items.why: Paper loses strength because water loosens the joins between its fibres. Plastic does not take in water, so it stays about the same. Cotton fibres hold together a little better when damp, so cotton gets a little stronger. That is why the spinners in the story worked in the damp morning air.
items.context: In the dry or damp test, you hang a bag from a strip or a thread and pour in water until it breaks. You compare dry and damp.

items.p: Long ago, traders in different towns used different weights for a 'kilogram'. Why does science use the same units everywhere?
items.a: If each person uses a different size of a unit, the same measure gives different numbers, and nobody can check or trust results. A shared unit means anyone can repeat the test and get the same answer. It is also fair for buyers and sellers.
items.why: Shared units make results comparable and honest.

items.p: A probe on the Moon measured the soil. It was about 70 degrees Celsius on top. It was about 10 degrees below zero just eight centimetres down. What does this show about Moon soil?
opts: It is a very good insulator of heat
It is a very good conductor of heat
items.why: If heat flowed easily through it, the top and the deeper layer would soon be about the same temperature. A huge difference in a few centimetres means heat flows very slowly. That is an insulator. Picking 'conductor' reverses it.
items.context: India's Chandrayaan-3 lander carried a probe in 2023. It pushed into the Moon soil near the south pole and measured the temperature at different depths.

items.p: A hard material can never be flexible.
items.why: False. A steel spring is hard to scratch, and it is also elastic. A thin plastic ruler is fairly hard and flexible. Hard means hard to scratch. Flexible means it bends without breaking. They are different properties, so a material can have any mix.

items.p: In the story, why was Shefali's test fair? Name two things she kept the same.
items.a: She cut every thread to the same length, her forearm's length. She used the same kind of shells, all the same size, one at a time. She used threads from the same ball of cotton. Only the time of day changed.
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Here it was the dampness of the air.
items.context: In the story The Thread That Held at Dawn, a girl hung threads and added cowrie shells until they broke. She did this at dawn and at noon.

items.p: A scientist says, 'Cotton thread is strong.' What should she add to be more accurate?
opts: How long and how thick the thread was, and how damp the air was
Nothing, because it is always true
items.why: A thread's strength depends on its thickness and on the dampness of the air. The same words 'cotton thread' could describe very different results. Picking 'nothing' is the idea that properties never change, which the story showed is wrong.

items.p: Agnes Pockels was not allowed to go to university. She measured water in her kitchen anyway. Why do you think she kept going, and what might the world have missed if she had stopped?
items.a: She was curious and she noticed something real, so she wanted to find out. If she had stopped, the study of how surfaces work might have started later. Soap, oils and the skins of cells all depend on it. Her letter to Lord Rayleigh also shows that asking an expert can open a door.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer gives a reason from her story. It also says what the world loses when people are kept out.

items.p: Nobody can touch nuclear pasta, a material that may exist inside a dead star. How can scientists say anything about it?
opts: They use computer models built on rules tested on Earth
They have a sample in a laboratory
They saw it through a telescope
items.why: Scientists use well-tested rules about atoms and forces and run them on powerful computers. This gives a prediction, not a proof. That is why it is marked as an idea. Picking 'a sample' is wrong, because no one has one.

items.p: Draw a zoom-in: a cotton thread, then one fibre, then a pattern of atoms joined together. Label the three pictures.
items.a: A thread made of many fibres twisted together. One fibre as a long thin strand. At the smallest scale, tiny balls joined in chains.
items.why: Properties come from small things joined in patterns. Each zoom-in shows a smaller building block.
items.art: Three blank circles joined by arrows.

items.p: Which one is a property of the material, and not just of the object?
opts: It is shaped like a bowl
items.why: Hard to scratch is true of the steel itself, in any shape. Being shaped like a bowl, being in a kitchen and being bought last year describe the one object only. Picking shape is the common mix-up between a material and an object.
items.context: A material is what a thing is made of. An object is one thing with a shape and a use.

items.p: A glass bangle is hard and brittle. A steel spoon is hard and strong. Which would you choose for a bridge, and why? Which would you choose for a window, and why?
items.a: For a bridge, steel, because it must not snap when heavy things pass. For a window, glass, because it is see-through. Steel is not see-through, and glass would shatter on a bridge.
items.why: Each job needs a different set of properties. A good answer names the property for each job.

items.p: Invent a new material for a school bag. List three properties it should have and say how you would test each one.
items.a: Strong: hang a bag from a strip and pour in water cup by cup until it tears. Waterproof: drip water on it and see if it stays dry underneath after five minutes. Light: weigh the same size piece on a kitchen scale. Any three properties with a sensible test are right.
items.why: Inventing a material means knowing the properties you want and being able to test for them.

experiments.title: Snap, Bend or Spring Back?
experiments.question: When we push a thing past its limit, does it snap, stay bent, or spring back?
experiments.predict: Before you test anything, put the eight things into three piles: SNAPS, STAYS BENT and SPRINGS BACK. Which pile does each one go in, and why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, bend every thing slowly, with two hands, the same way each time. Use a new piece each time, because a bent piece is not the same any more. Do each test twice.
results_table: Bend a little: does it spring back?

materials.item: a dry spaghetti stick, and a few more as spares
2 sticks of chalk
2 ice cream sticks
a thin plastic ruler
a large paper clip
a strip of kitchen foil, 2 centimetres by 15 centimetres
a stick of plasticine or dough
a rubber band
a clear plastic bag or a folded towel, to catch the pieces
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Bend things inside the plastic bag or folded towel, so that no pieces fly. Wear glasses if you have them. A grown-up bends the paper clip, because the wire ends can poke. Bend the plastic ruler only into a gentle curve. Never stretch a rubber band until it snaps.

schedule.what: Guess the piles. Bend each thing a little, then more. Write what happens. Sort them into groups.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write the name of each group under its things.
experiments.context: This is the bend test. You bend or stretch eight things a little, then more, and watch what each does. Some snap, some stay bent and some spring back. This shows three different ways that materials behave.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the eight things. 2. Ask your child to make three piles on the table: SNAPS, STAYS BENT and SPRINGS BACK. 3. Ask them to say why for each.
flow.say: Imagine bending each of these. Some will snap. Some will stay bent. Some will spring back. Put each one in the pile you think it belongs to.
flow.kid: Look at the eight things. Make three piles. SNAPS, STAYS BENT and SPRINGS BACK. This is your guess.

ask.q: Why did you put that one in that pile?
good: It is dry and stiff, so it will snap.
It is metal, so it will stay bent.
It is rubber, so it will spring back.

flow.context: This is the first step of the bend test. You find out how different materials behave when pushed too far. First you guess.

flow.do: 1. Put the first thing inside the bag or towel. 2. Hold it with two hands. 3. Bend it a very little, and let go. Does it spring back? 4. Then bend it slowly more and more until something happens. 5. Bend the ruler only into a gentle curve, about a hand-width deep. 6. For the rubber band, stretch it to double its length and let go. Do not stretch it more.
flow.say: First bend it just a little and let go. Does it spring back? Then bend it more. Slowly. Does it snap? Does it stay bent? Watch carefully.
flow.kid: Bend a little and let go. Does it spring back? Then bend more, slowly. What happens?
flow.parent: A grown-up should do the paper clip. If a thing snaps, count the pieces. Write the number in the table.

flow.do: Test each of the eight things. Do each one twice, with a new piece if the first one broke. Write what happens in the table.
flow.say: Test all eight. Do each twice. Write down what you see. For the spaghetti, count the pieces.
flow.kid: Test all eight things, twice each. Write what happens. Count the pieces of the spaghetti.

chart.title: Made-up example results: what happened to each thing

flow.parent: Dry spaghetti rarely breaks into just two pieces. The story goes that the physicist Richard Feynman once spent an evening trying to break one stick into exactly two. He could not. Two scientists, Basile Audoly and Sebastien Neukirch, worked out why in 2005. When the stick snaps, the bend suddenly straightens. This sends a wave along the stick that bends it so much that it snaps again. They won a funny science prize, the Ig Nobel Prize, for this in 2006. If you bend a paper clip back and forth many times, you will feel it get warm, then it snaps. Your bending has put energy into the metal as heat.

flow.do: Look at the table. Sort the eight things into three groups. Say a word for each group.
flow.say: Look at your results. Which things snapped? Which stayed bent? Which sprang back? A thing that snaps is called brittle. A thing that springs back is called elastic.
flow.kid: Sort your results into three groups. Things that snap are brittle. Things that spring back are elastic.

check.q: Dry spaghetti snaps when bent. Chalk snaps. What word describes them both?
check.why: Brittle means it snaps or shatters instead of bending. Elastic means it springs back. Flexible means it bends easily. Spaghetti and chalk do not bend much before they break, so they are brittle. Picking 'flexible' means thinking that snapping is a kind of bending.

flow.do: Talk about what the things in each group have in common. Ask: why does metal stay bent, but a plastic ruler spring back?
flow.say: Look at the thing that stayed bent, and the thing that sprang back. Both bend. What is different about them?
flow.kid: Both bent. One stayed bent. One sprang back. What is different?
flow.think: Inside a paper clip, the tiny atoms slide to new places and stay there. Inside a ruler, long chains bend a little and spring home. Why might a snap be different?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: dry things snap, metals stay bent and rubbery things spring back. What I saw: the spaghetti snapped into three pieces, the paper clip stayed bent and the ruler sprang back. Why: a brittle thing cannot give, so it breaks. Metals let their atoms slide. Elastic things stretch and spring home.

experiments.title: The Droop Test: how flexible is it?
experiments.question: Which strips bend the most when they stick out from a table, and which bend the least?
experiments.predict: Line up the strips. Put the one you think is the most rigid first, and the most flexible last. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, cut every strip 2 centimetres wide and 20 centimetres long. Let exactly 10 centimetres stick out over the edge. Tape the same coin to the tip of each. Measure each strip 3 times.

materials.item: strips 2 centimetres wide and 20 centimetres long: corrugated card from a carton, thin card from a cereal or sweet box, printer paper, newspaper, kitchen foil folded in three, and cotton cloth
one coin, such as a 1 rupee coin, the same one every time
sticky tape
a heavy book to hold the strip down
a 30 centimetre ruler
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Cut the strips with child scissors, or ask a grown-up to cut the card. Do not use anything sharp or splintery.

schedule.what: Guess the order. Measure the drop of each strip 3 times. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart. Draw one bar for each strip. Make each bar as tall as the middle value.
experiments.context: This is the droop test. You push a strip of material out over the edge of a table, and measure how far its tip drops. A big drop means a flexible material. A small drop means a rigid one.

flow.do: 1. Lay the six strips out. 2. Ask your child to put them in a line, the most rigid first and the most flexible last. 3. Ask why.
flow.say: Which strip will stay straightest when it sticks out? Which will bend the most? Put them in a line. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put the six strips in a line. Stiffest first, floppiest last. Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the droop test. You find out how flexible each strip is by letting it stick out over a table edge.

flow.do: 1. Lay the first strip on the table. 2. Slide it until exactly 10 centimetres stick out over the edge. 3. Put the heavy book on the other end. 4. Tape the coin to the tip.
flow.say: We let 10 centimetres stick out each time, with the same coin on the tip. Only the strip changes. That makes it a fair test.
flow.kid: Put a strip on the table with 10 centimetres sticking out. Hold the other end under a book. Tape the coin to the tip.
flow.parent: Draw a pencil line across each strip, 10 centimetres from its end. Line it up with the table edge each time.

flow.do: 1. Hold the ruler upright, just beside the tip of the strip. 2. Put its 0 mark level with the table top. 3. Bend down so your eyes are level with the tip. 4. Read how far the tip has dropped. 5. Do this 3 times for each strip. If a strip hangs straight down, write 10.
flow.say: The drop is how far the tip goes down from the table top. A small drop means rigid. A big drop means flexible.
flow.kid: Hold the ruler upright by the tip. Read how far it dropped. Do it 3 times.

chart.title: A ruler, reading the drop of a paper strip in centimetres (cm)
chart.label: Read where the tip of the strip reaches on the ruler.

flow.parent: To find the middle value, put the three numbers in order and take the middle one. If one try is very different, check the length sticking out. Check that the coin was in the same place.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the middle values, with one bar for each strip.
flow.say: Each strip gets one bar. The taller the bar, the more the strip bent down.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each strip. A taller bar means a more flexible strip.

check.q: In the droop test, a strip with a big drop is…
check.why: A big drop means the strip bent a lot under the coin. That is a flexible strip. A small drop means rigid. Picking 'stronger' mixes up flexible and strong. A very flexible cloth can still be strong.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how far the tip of each strip dropped
chart.note: These numbers are made up. The most a strip can drop here is 10 centimetres, because that is how far it sticks out.

flow.do: Talk about the corrugated card, the thin card and the paper. They are all made of wood fibres. What changed?
flow.say: Card is made of the same wood fibres as paper. But it bends much less. What is different about it?
flow.kid: Card and paper are both made of wood fibres. Why does card bend less?
flow.think: Thickness matters as well as material. How could you test a thick and a thin strip of the same paper?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the corrugated card is the most rigid and the cloth is the most flexible. What I saw: the card dropped 1 centimetre and the cloth hung straight down at 10. Why: thick card has many layers of fibres pressed together, and cloth threads can slide and fold.

experiments.title: Dry or Damp? Does water change how strong it is?
experiments.question: When paper or cotton thread gets damp, does it get stronger, weaker or stay the same?
experiments.predict: For each of the three materials, guess: will the damp one hold more cups of water than the dry one, fewer, or the same? And why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, cut each kind of strip to the same size every time, and cut the newspaper strips in the same direction. Hang every strip the same way. Pour with the same cup, one cupful at a time. Make every damp strip damp in the same way, right across its middle with a wet fingertip. Test each one twice.

materials.item: toilet paper: 4 strips, each the full width of the roll and 2 sheets long. Put a piece of sticky tape across the dotted tear line, on both sides, so the strip does not tear there.
newspaper: 4 strips, each 1 centimetre wide and 25 centimetres long, all cut in the same direction, down the length of the page
cotton sewing thread from a reel: 4 pieces, each 1 metre long. Each one is folded in half to make a doubled thread. Check that the reel says cotton.
a broom handle or a long stick, laid across the backs of two chairs
a pencil, or a wooden spoon if the pencil starts to bend
sticky tape
a thin plastic carry bag with handles and no holes
a cup that holds about 200 millilitres, like a tea cup or a small steel tumbler, the same one every time
a jug or large bottle of water, and a small bowl of water for wetting a finger
a bucket, to stand under the bag
a pen and the results table

experiments.safety: Stand the bucket under the bag, so the water falls into it. Wipe up any spills at once, so no one slips. Keep the bag away from babies and toddlers.

schedule.what: Guess. Test dry and damp toilet paper, newspaper and cotton thread. Compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. In the last column, write weaker, stronger or about the same.
experiments.context: In this experiment you hang a plastic bag from a strip of paper or a cotton thread. You pour water into the bag, one cup at a time, until the strip tears. You do it with dry strips, then with damp ones. It shows whether water changes how strong a material is.

flow.do: 1. Show the toilet paper, the newspaper and the thread. 2. For each one, ask your child to guess: will the damp one hold more water, less, or the same? 3. Ask why.
flow.say: Think of wet newspaper. Is it stronger or weaker than dry newspaper? What about wet thread? Guess for each one, and tell me why.
flow.kid: Look at the three materials. Will the damp one hold more, less or the same? Why?

ask.q: Why did you guess that for the thread?
good: Wet paper tears, so wet thread might break too.
Wet cloth feels heavy and tough.
I am not sure. We have to test it.

flow.context: This is the first step of Dry or Damp. You will find out whether getting damp makes a material stronger or weaker. First you guess.

flow.do: 1. Put two chairs back to back, a little apart. Lay the broom handle across their backs. 2. Wrap the top of a dry toilet paper strip once round the handle, and tape it to itself. 3. Wrap the bottom end round the pencil and tape it. 4. Hang the bag's two handles on the two ends of the pencil. 5. Stand the bucket under the bag.
flow.say: The bag hangs from the strip. We pour in water one cup at a time. The more cups it holds before it tears, the stronger the strip.
flow.kid: Hang the strip from the stick. Hang the bag from the pencil. Put the bucket below.
flow.parent: For the thread, fold one piece in half. Put the pencil through the loop at the bottom. Tie the two loose ends round the broom handle with a double knot. Two strands make the thread strong enough to hold at least a cup. If the tape slips instead of the strip tearing, do not count that try. Tape it more firmly and start again.
flow.context: This step sets up the Dry or Damp test. A strip hangs from a stick, and a bag hangs from the strip.

flow.do: 1. Fill the cup to the brim and pour it gently into the bag. Count out loud. 2. Keep adding one cup at a time. 3. When the strip tears, write down how many cups were in the bag. 4. Empty the bag and test the second dry strip. 5. Then test the dry newspaper and the dry thread the same way, twice each.
flow.say: Pour gently, so the bag does not swing. Count each cup out loud. When the strip tears, write down the number.
flow.kid: Pour one cup at a time and count. Write the number when it tears.
flow.parent: If a strip or thread holds 10 cups and is still there, write 'more than 10' and stop, because the bag may get too full. Pouring with a jerk can tear a strip early. Pour slowly, every time.
flow.context: In this step you test the dry strips. You pour water into the hanging bag until each strip tears.

flow.do: 1. Hang a new dry strip with the empty bag, as before. 2. Dip a fingertip in the bowl of water. 3. Dab the middle of the strip, right across from edge to edge. Stop when a band about 3 centimetres tall looks dark and damp. For the thread, run a wet finger along the middle of both strands. 4. Wait one minute. 5. Pour in water, one cup at a time, and write the number when it tears. 6. Do each material twice.
flow.say: Now we make the middle of each strip damp, not dripping. Then we pour, just like before. Watch what happens.
flow.kid: Wet your fingertip. Touch the middle of the strip. Then pour and count.
flow.parent: Make the damp band go right across the strip. If one edge stays dry, the dry part still holds the bag. If a damp toilet paper strip tears before any water goes in, write 0. That is a real result. We hang the strip first and dampen it after, because a damp strip is hard to hang without tearing.
flow.context: In this step you make each strip damp in the middle, then test it the same way as the dry strips.

flow.do: Help your child fill in the last column, then compare the changes.
flow.say: For each material, look at dry and damp. Write weaker, stronger or about the same. Which one changed the most?
flow.kid: Look at dry and damp for each one. Write weaker, stronger or the same.
flow.parent: Your numbers depend on your paper, your thread and your cup, so they will not match anyone else's. With a cup of about 200 millilitres, expect roughly this. Dry toilet paper holds about 1 to 6 cups, and dry newspaper about 2 to 10. Both damp papers usually tear before the second cup, often before the first. Paper is held together by joins where its fibres touch, and water loosens these joins. The doubled thread usually holds about 2 to 7 cups, dry or damp. Textile scientists find damp cotton is about one tenth to one fifth stronger. A change that small may not show when you count whole cups, so 'about the same' is an honest result.

check.q: A newspaper strip held 6 cups of water when dry and 1 cup when damp. What can you say?
options: Water made the newspaper much weaker
Damp newspaper is stronger because water is heavy
check.why: 6 cups dry and only 1 cup damp, so the damp strip held 5 cups less. Water loosens the joins between the paper fibres, so they pull apart easily. Picking 'water is heavy' mixes up the weight of the water with the strength of the paper.

chart.title: Made-up example results: cups of water held, dry and damp

flow.context: In this step you compare the dry and damp results for each material.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: water makes paper much weaker, but not cotton thread. What I saw: the dry toilet paper held 4 cups, and the damp one tore with none. The thread held 5 cups dry and 5 damp. Why: paper is held together where its fibres touch, and water loosens those joins. Thread is held together by its twist. Damp cotton fibres swell a little and grip each other harder, so the thread does not get weaker.
flow.think: Damp cotton thread did not get weaker. Why might this matter to someone who spins very fine cotton thread?

experiments.title: The Vanishing Drop: how fast does it soak in?
experiments.question: How many seconds does one drop of water take to vanish on each surface? Which surfaces never let it in?
experiments.predict: Line up the six surfaces. Put the one you think soaks up a drop fastest first, and the one that never soaks it up last. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, make every drop the same size, using the same dropper or the same spoon tip. Place each drop in a fresh spot. Stop at 120 seconds if the drop is still there. Test each surface 3 times.

materials.item: flat pieces of paper towel, cotton cloth, newspaper, printer paper, butter paper and a plastic carry bag
a dropper, or a spoon with a small tip
a cup of water
a plate to rest the pieces on
a watch or phone with seconds
a colocasia (arbi) leaf, if you have one
black pepper and a drop of dish soap
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Wipe up spilt water so no one slips.

schedule.what: Guess the order. Time one drop on each surface 3 times. Draw a bar chart. Try the pepper and soap trick.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart. Draw one bar for each surface. Make each bar as tall as the middle value in seconds.
experiments.context: In this experiment you put one drop of water on each of six surfaces. You time how long it takes to vanish. A short time means the surface is absorbent. A drop that never vanishes means the surface is waterproof.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the six pieces. 2. Ask your child to put them in a line, fastest-soaking first.
flow.say: Which surface will soak up a drop the fastest? Which will never soak it up? Put them in a line, fastest first. Why that order?
flow.kid: Look at the six surfaces. Put them in a line. Fastest to soak first. This is your guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the vanishing drop test. You find out which materials are absorbent and which are waterproof, by timing a drop.

flow.do: 1. Lay the first piece flat on the plate. 2. Make one drop from the dropper. 3. Start the timer the moment the drop touches. 4. Look from the side. 5. Stop the timer when the shiny drop is gone.
flow.say: Put one drop on the surface and start the timer at once. Watch from the side. Stop when the shiny drop has gone into the material.
flow.kid: Put one drop on a piece. Start the timer. Stop when the shiny drop is gone.
flow.parent: If the drop is still sitting there after 120 seconds, stop and write 120. That is a result, and it means the surface is waterproof. Use a fresh spot for each try.

flow.do: Test each surface 3 times, in fresh places. Write down the seconds each time.
flow.say: Do all six surfaces, three tries each. Write the seconds. For the plastic, write 120 if the drop is still there.
flow.kid: Test each surface three times. Write the seconds. If the drop is still there after 120, write 120.
flow.parent: To find the middle value, put the three numbers in order and take the middle one. If one try is very different, check that the drop was the same size.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the middle values, with one bar for each surface.
flow.say: Each surface gets one bar. A short bar means the drop vanished fast. A tall bar means it took a long time or never went in.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each surface. A short bar means the drop soaked in fast.

check.q: In the vanishing drop chart, a very tall bar means the surface is…
check.why: A tall bar is a long time. The drop stayed on top for a long time or never went in. That is waterproof. Picking 'very absorbent' reads the chart backwards. The most absorbent surface has the shortest bar, because its drop vanishes fastest.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how many seconds one drop of water took to vanish
chart.note: These numbers are made up. A bar of 120 means the drop was still there after 2 minutes, when we stopped.

flow.do: Fill a plate with water. Shake pepper onto it. Dip a finger in dish soap and touch the middle. Also look at a drop on a colocasia leaf, if you have one.
flow.say: Pepper floats on the water. Now touch the middle with a soapy finger. What happens? The surface of water acts like a thin, stretchy skin. Soap weakens it.
flow.kid: Sprinkle pepper on a plate of water. Touch the middle with a soapy finger. Watch the pepper!
flow.parent: The pepper rushes to the edge. The skin of water, called surface tension, is weaker where the soap touches. The stronger skin around pulls the pepper away. The same skin is why a drop is round on the colocasia leaf. The leaf is covered with tiny wax bumps, so the water cannot spread. The testing-materials unit tells the story of Agnes Pockels, who studied this skin in her kitchen.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: paper towel is the most absorbent and plastic is waterproof. What I saw: the drop vanished in 2 seconds on paper towel. It was still there after 120 seconds on plastic. Why: the paper towel has tiny gaps that pull water in, and plastic has no gaps.

experiments.title: Layers to Darkness: transparent, translucent or opaque?
experiments.question: How many layers of each material does it take to stop a torch's light?
experiments.predict: Guess how many layers of butter paper it will take before the light disappears from the wall. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same torch, the same wall distance and the same dim room each time. Add one layer at a time. Count the layers when the light spot on the wall just disappears.

materials.item: a torch
a plain wall in a dim room, or in the evening
15 sheets of butter paper or tracing paper
10 sheets of tissue paper
a thin cotton cloth, and some sheets of newspaper
a clear glass or plastic cup, a steel plate and a piece of cardboard
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Do not shine the torch into anyone's eyes.

schedule.what: Sort the materials with a torch. Then add layers until the light disappears. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart. Draw one bar for each material. Make each bar as tall as the number of layers.
experiments.context: In this experiment you shine a torch through different materials onto a wall. First you sort them as transparent, translucent or opaque. Then you add layers one at a time to see how many it takes to block the light.

flow.do: 1. Dim the room. 2. Shine the torch on the wall. 3. Hold each thing in front of the torch. Try the cup, the butter paper, the cloth, the steel plate and the cardboard. 4. Sort each one: transparent, translucent or opaque.
flow.say: Hold each thing in front of the torch. Transparent means a clear bright spot. Translucent means a blurry glow. Opaque means just a shadow.
flow.kid: Hold each thing in front of the torch. Is the spot on the wall clear, blurry or gone? Sort them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the layers experiment. You use a torch to sort materials into transparent, translucent and opaque.
flow.parent: Good answers: the cup is transparent. The butter paper and thin cloth are translucent. The steel plate and cardboard are opaque.

flow.do: 1. Hold one sheet of butter paper flat against the front of the torch. 2. Look at the glow on the wall. 3. Add a second sheet. 4. Keep adding, one at a time, counting, until you cannot see any glow on the wall.
flow.say: Add one sheet at a time and watch the glow. Count the sheets. Stop when the light spot is just gone.
flow.kid: Add one sheet at a time. Count them. Stop when the light is gone.

ask.q: What do you notice as you add more layers?
good: The light gets dimmer.
The glow gets smaller.
It goes from translucent to opaque.

flow.parent: If you use up all your sheets and a glow still shows, write 'more than' and the number of sheets. That is a real result. A bright torch may need many sheets.

flow.do: Repeat with tissue paper, thin cloth and newspaper. Write down the number of layers for each.
flow.say: Now do the same with tissue paper, cloth and newspaper. Which one blocks the light with the fewest layers?
flow.kid: Do the same with tissue paper, cloth and newspaper. Count the layers each time.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the layers for each material.
flow.say: Each material gets a bar. A taller bar means it took more layers to block the light.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each material. A taller bar means more layers.

check.q: One sheet of butter paper is translucent. A tall stack is opaque. What does this show?
options: Translucent or opaque can depend on thickness
check.why: Each layer scatters and soaks up some light. One layer leaves lots, so it is translucent. A tall stack leaves none, so it is opaque. Picking 'the atoms change' is a nice thought, but the atoms are the same. We simply added more of them in the way of the light.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how many layers it took to block the torch light
chart.y: Layers until no light came through
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different, and depend on your torch and your paper.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: more layers make a material more opaque. What I saw: one butter paper let a glow through, but 5 layers stopped it. Why: each layer scatters and soaks up some light, so the more layers there are, the less gets through.

activities.title: Feely Bag Detective

materials.item: a cloth bag or pillowcase
8 small things: a steel spoon, a wooden spoon, a rubber band, a cotton ball, a smooth stone, a plastic bottle cap, a sponge, a key
a room thermometer, if you have one. A fever thermometer will not work, because it only reads near body temperature.

activities.safety: Use nothing sharp or breakable. Keep the small things away from babies and toddlers.

schedule.what: Describe things by touch, using only property words. Then guess.

activities.record: Write down the three property words that gave the best clue for each thing.
activities.context: In this game you feel things you cannot see, inside a bag, and describe them with property words only. A friend then guesses what they are.

flow.do: 1. Put the eight things in the bag without your child looking. 2. Explain: they will feel one thing at a time and describe it only with property words. They may not say what it is.
flow.say: Put a hand in the bag and feel one thing. Tell me what it is like. You may say hard, soft, cold, smooth, rough or flexible. You may not say its name.
flow.kid: Feel one thing in the bag. Tell what it is like. Do not say its name.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Feely Bag Detective game. You use only touch, and property words, to describe hidden things.

flow.do: 1. Your child describes a thing in the bag using only property words. 2. You guess what it is. 3. Swap roles. 4. Play until all 8 things are out.
flow.say: Tell me three things about it. Hard or soft? Smooth or rough? Cold or warm? Then I will guess.
flow.kid: Describe the thing with three property words. Your partner guesses. Then swap.

good: Cold and hard together tell it is metal.
Flexible and springy tell it is rubber.
Soft and fluffy tell it is cotton.

flow.parent: Praise exact words. 'Smooth, cold, hard' is better than 'nice'. If your child stops at one word, ask for two more.

flow.do: Take out the steel spoon and the wooden spoon. Ask your child to hold one in each hand, eyes closed. Ask which feels colder. If you have a room thermometer, read it. Both spoons have been in this room all day, so both are at this temperature.
flow.say: Hold one in each hand. Which feels colder? Now open your eyes. Have they been in the same room all day?
flow.kid: Hold a steel spoon in one hand. Hold a wooden spoon in the other. Which feels colder?

check.q: A steel spoon feels colder than a wooden spoon, in the same room. What does that tell you?
options: Steel carries heat away from your hand faster
check.why: Both are at room temperature. Steel takes heat from your hand faster than wood does, so your skin says 'cold'. Picking 'steel is a lower temperature' is the common idea. A thermometer would show the same number for both. Wood makes no heat of its own.

flow.do: Talk about which senses helped. Touch was used here, but ask what other senses could tell us about a material.
flow.say: We used touch. What other senses help us find out about a material? What can looking tell us? Listening?
flow.kid: Touch told us a lot. What could your eyes and ears tell you about a material?
flow.think: Your skin said the steel was cold. Was your skin right or wrong?

setup.caption: 2. Tell what it is like. Do not say its name.

activities.title: The Property Passport

materials.item: a steel tumbler or tiffin box
a tawa or frying pan with a wooden or plastic handle, or a photo of one
a sheet of paper folded into a small booklet
a pencil

schedule.what: Fill in a property passport for one object. Then find the two materials in a frying pan.

activities.record: A passport page for one object, with the answer to each question.
activities.context: In this activity you make a passport for one everyday object. You find out its properties, one by one, and learn the difference between an object and its material.

flow.do: 1. Fold the paper into a booklet. 2. Choose the steel tumbler. 3. On the first page write: Object: steel tumbler. Material: steel.
flow.say: An object is a single thing with a shape and a use. A material is what it is made of. Let's write both on the first page.
flow.kid: Choose the steel tumbler. Write: Object, steel tumbler. Material, steel.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Property Passport. A passport tells you about a traveller. This one tells you about a material.
flow.parent: Say again, in plain words: the tumbler is the object. Steel is the material. The tumbler's shape is a property of the object. The steel's properties would be the same in a spoon or a sheet.

flow.do: Fill in the passport with these questions. Hard or soft? Rigid or flexible? Shiny or dull? Rough or smooth? See-through or not? Waterproof or absorbent? Cold to touch or not? Does it ring when tapped? Does it float? Write one answer for each.
flow.say: Let's ask the tumbler these questions one by one. For each, look, touch or try it. Then write the answer.
flow.kid: Ask the tumbler each question. Look, touch or try it. Write the answers in the passport.
flow.parent: Expected answers for steel: hard, rigid, shiny, smooth, opaque and waterproof. It feels cold and rings when tapped. An empty tumbler floats if you set it down gently, upright, on a bucket of water. A solid lump of steel would sink.

flow.do: Now look at the frying pan. Ask: how many materials is it made of? Make a passport entry for each one.
flow.say: A frying pan has a metal body and a wooden or plastic handle. Two materials in one object. Do they have the same properties?
flow.kid: Look at the pan. It has two materials. Write a passport entry for each.

ask.q: Why are the two materials different?
good: The pan must carry heat to the food, so it is metal.
The handle must not carry heat to my hand, so it is wood or plastic.

check.q: A frying pan has a metal body and a wooden handle. Which is true?
options: One object, two materials, with different properties
check.why: The pan is one object. It is made of two materials, metal and wood. They have different properties, and that is why each is used where it is. Picking 'one material' misses the wood. The object and its materials are different ideas.

flow.do: Ask your child to choose another object at home and make a passport at another time.
flow.say: Which object would you like to make a passport for next? Look for one with more than one material.
flow.kid: Pick another object at home. Make a passport for it later.
flow.think: Which property did you find hardest to decide? Why was it hard?

activities.title: The Property Ladder

materials.item: a piece of string and some clothes pegs
6 small things from home, such as a steel spoon, a wooden spoon, a piece of chalk, a rubber (eraser), a cotton cloth, a plastic ruler
a new steel nail, handled by a grown-up
a magnifying glass
paper labels and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up handles the nail. Use nothing sharp or breakable.

schedule.what: Put six things in order on a washing-line ladder for three properties. See how the order changes.

activities.record: Draw your three ladders and write the six things in order on each.
activities.context: In this activity you put the same six things in order on a line, three times. Each time you use a different property: hardness, how flexible it is, and roughness. You find that the order changes with the property.

flow.do: 1. Stretch a string across a doorway like a washing line. 2. Label one end 'hardest' and the other end 'softest'. 3. Show your child the fingernail test: try to scratch the thing with your fingernail. If it scratches, the thing is soft. If it does not, try the nail, with a grown-up.
flow.say: We will put these six things in order from hardest to softest. First try your fingernail on each one. If it scratches, the thing is soft. If not, ask a grown-up to try the nail.
flow.kid: Stretch the string. One end is hardest. The other is softest. Try your fingernail on each thing.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Property Ladder. You put things in order on a line, from most to least of one property. Here the property is hardness.
flow.parent: This is a small version of the Scratch Ladder in the unit Sorting materials, which does the full test. Here we only need three groups: scratched by a fingernail, scratched only by a nail, and not scratched by either.

flow.do: 1. Your child pegs the six things on the line in order of hardness. 2. Test any pair that is hard to decide by trying to scratch one with the other. 3. Draw the ladder.
flow.say: Is the chalk harder than the rubber? How can you check? Test each pair you are not sure of.
flow.kid: Peg the things in order, hardest to softest. Test any pair you are unsure about.

ask.q: How did you decide where each thing goes?
good: I scratched it with my nail.
I tried to scratch one with another.
It dents when I press it.

flow.parent: If two things seem equal, peg them side by side. Ties are fine.

flow.do: 1. Take the things down. 2. Peg them again in order of how flexible they are: the most flexible at one end. 3. Then again in order of roughness, using a magnifying glass to look at each surface.
flow.say: Now do the ladder again, but this time put the most flexible first. Then again for the roughest. Does the order stay the same?
flow.kid: Make the ladder again. This time for flexible. Then for rough. Does the order change?

check.q: A steel spoon is near the top of the hardness ladder. Where is it on the flexible ladder?
options: In the same place as on the hardness ladder
check.why: A steel spoon is hard and rigid. It sits at the hard end of one ladder and the rigid end of the other. But a rubber is soft and flexible. A plastic ruler is fairly hard and flexible. So the orders are not the same. Picking 'same place' misses that each property has its own ladder.

flow.do: Compare the three ladders. Ask: which thing moved the most? Which stayed in about the same place?
flow.say: Look at your three ladders. Which thing moved the most from one ladder to the next? Which stayed put?
flow.kid: Compare the three ladders. Which thing moved the most? Which stayed put?
flow.think: If every property gave the same ladder, would we need more than one word? What does that tell you?

flow.do: Ask your child to say one sentence for each ladder, starting with 'The ... is harder than the ...'
flow.say: Say one sentence for each ladder. For example: the steel spoon is harder than the wooden spoon.
flow.kid: Say one sentence for each ladder. Start with 'The … is …er than the …'.
flow.parent: Using 'harder than' and 'more flexible than' is the language of comparing. Numbers come next, in the experiments.

activities.title: Through Coloured Plastic

materials.item: red, green and blue see-through plastic, from sweet wrappers, cellophane or a coloured file cover
a torch
a sheet of white paper or a plain wall
a picture with red, green and blue things, such as a flower, a leaf and a toy
sticky tape

activities.safety: Do not shine the torch into anyone's eyes. Never look at the Sun through anything.

schedule.what: Look at a picture through coloured plastic. Then shine a torch through it onto a wall.

activities.record: Draw the picture as it looked through each colour. Write what you noticed.
activities.context: In this activity you look at the world through see-through coloured plastic. You find out that a coloured see-through material lets some colours of light through and soaks up the others.

flow.do: 1. Hold the red plastic up to your eye and look at the picture. 2. Note how each thing looks. 3. Do the same with green, then blue.
flow.say: Look at the picture through the red plastic. What happens to the red things? What happens to the green things? Now try green and blue.
flow.kid: Look at the picture through the red plastic. What happens to each colour? Now try green. Now blue.
flow.context: This is the first step of Through Coloured Plastic. A see-through coloured material, like a sweet wrapper, changes the colours you see through it.
flow.parent: Through red plastic, red things and white paper look bright red, and green and blue things look dark. The red plastic lets red light through and soaks up most of the other colours.

flow.do: 1. Dim the room. 2. Tape the red plastic over the torch. 3. Shine it on white paper. 4. Try green and blue the same way. 5. Then hold the red and the green together over the torch.
flow.say: White light is all the colours of the rainbow mixed. Red plastic lets only the red through. Try red, then green, then both together. What happens when both are in front of the torch?
flow.kid: Cover the torch with red plastic. Shine it on white paper. Try green and blue. Then use red and green together.

check.q: You hold a red plastic and a green plastic together in front of a torch. What do you see on the wall?
options: Almost no light, because each one blocks what the other lets through
check.why: The red plastic lets red light through and soaks up green. The green plastic lets green through and soaks up red. Together they let almost nothing through. Picking 'yellow' comes from shining a red light and a green light on the same spot, which does make yellow. But filters work by taking colours away, not adding them.

flow.do: Talk about why the same light looks red through red plastic. Ask where the other colours went.
flow.say: White light has all the colours in it. The red plastic lets the red through. Where did the other colours go?
flow.kid: The red plastic let only red through. Where did the other colours go?

ask.q: Where do the other colours go?
good: The plastic soaks them up.
They turn into a tiny bit of heat in the plastic.

flow.parent: Soaked-up light turns into a very small amount of heat. This is why a dark coloured cloth feels warmer in the sun than a white one.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the picture as it looked through each colour. Ask which plastic made each thing look darkest.
flow.say: Draw what you saw through each colour. Which thing looked darkest through the red plastic?
flow.kid: Draw the picture as it looked through each colour.
flow.think: Is red plastic transparent, translucent or opaque? Is it the same for every colour of light?

activities.title: Dance of the Three Veils

materials.item: a clear plastic sheet or a very thin chiffon dupatta
a cotton dupatta or a sheet of butter paper
a tray or a sheet of cardboard
music

activities.safety: Clear a space so no one trips. Do not wrap a veil around anyone's head.

schedule.what: Dance behind three different veils and call the words.

activities.record: Draw the three veils and write transparent, translucent or opaque under each.
activities.context: In this movement game you dance behind three different veils. You feel what transparent, translucent and opaque mean with your whole body.

flow.do: 1. Give your child the three props. 2. Explain the three calls. CLEAR means dance behind the clear sheet. MIST means dance behind the cotton. HIDE means dance behind the tray.
flow.say: When I call 'clear', dance behind the clear sheet. When I call 'mist', dance behind the cotton. When I call 'hide', dance behind the tray.
flow.kid: Three calls. CLEAR, MIST, HIDE. Each one means a different veil.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dance of the Three Veils. A veil is a thin cloth held in front of you. Each veil shows light in a different way.

flow.do: 1. Play music. 2. Call the words in any order. 3. Your child dances behind the right veil. 4. You watch and say what you can see of them.
flow.say: Behind the clear sheet, I can see everything. Behind the cotton, I see a shape. Behind the tray, I see nothing. Let us dance!
flow.kid: Dance behind the veil you are called to. Your partner tells what they can see.

ask.q: What could I see through each veil?
good: Clear: everything.
Mist: only a blurry shape.
Hide: nothing at all.

flow.do: Swap. Your child calls the words and you dance. Talk about what changed.
flow.say: Now you call, and I will dance. Which veil is best for hiding? Which is best for watching?
flow.kid: Swap places. You call the words now.

check.q: Early morning fog is thin. You can see a tree through it, but it looks blurry. Fog is…
check.why: Light gets through the fog but is scattered, so the tree looks blurry. That is translucent. Thin air would be transparent. Very thick fog can become almost opaque. Picking 'transparent' means thinking blurry is the same as clear.

flow.do: Draw the three veils and write transparent, translucent or opaque under each.
flow.say: Draw the three veils. Write a word under each one.
flow.kid: Draw the three veils. Write a word under each.
flow.think: Which of the three would you choose for a window? Which for a curtain? Which for a door?

activities.title: The Kitchen Float Lab

materials.item: a big bowl or bucket of water
a cork, a steel nail, a plastic lid, a stone, a grape, a wooden spoon, an orange with its peel on
two same-sized pieces of kitchen foil, and a lump of plasticine or dough
a towel

activities.safety: Wipe up spilt water. A child should never be left alone near a bucket of water.

schedule.what: Guess float or sink. Test each thing. Then change a material's shape and test again.

activities.record: Make a table: thing, my guess, what happened.
activities.context: In this activity you guess whether things will float or sink in water, and then test them. You also find out that the same material can float in one shape and sink in another.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bowl with water. 2. Lay the things out. 3. For each thing, your child guesses: float or sink. 4. Write the guesses in a table.
flow.say: Here are some things. For each one, guess: will it float or will it sink? Write your guess down.
flow.kid: Look at each thing. Guess: float or sink? Write your guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Kitchen Float Lab. Float means stays on top of water. Sink means goes to the bottom.

flow.do: 1. Place each thing gently in the water, one at a time. 2. Watch and note what happens. 3. Write it in the table. 4. Peel the orange and test it again.
flow.say: Place each thing gently in the water. Does it float or sink? Peel the orange and try again. Surprised?
flow.kid: Test each thing. Write what happens. Then peel the orange and test it again.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.parent: An orange with its peel floats because the peel holds tiny pockets of air. Without the peel, it is more packed than water and sinks. Many children are surprised.

flow.do: 1. Roll one piece of foil into a tight ball. 2. Shape the other piece into a little boat with high sides. 3. Test both. 4. Do the same with the plasticine.
flow.say: Same foil, same weight. One ball, one boat. Which one will float? Try it.
flow.kid: Roll one piece of foil into a ball. Shape the other into a boat. Test both. What happens?

check.q: A foil ball sinks and a foil boat floats. Both are the same foil. Why?
options: The boat holds air, so it is less packed than water
The ball is a different material
check.why: The boat has a hollow space full of air. The boat and its air together are less packed than water. The ball is solid foil, more packed than water, so it sinks. They weigh the same, so 'lighter' is wrong. The material is the same, so 'different material' is wrong. The shape of the object is what changed.

flow.do: Talk about how a heavy steel ship floats. Ask your child to work out how it is like the foil boat.
flow.say: A ship weighs thousands of tonnes. But it floats. How is it like the foil boat?
flow.kid: A heavy steel ship floats. How is it like your foil boat?
flow.think: Ice floats on water. What does that tell you about how its pieces are packed?

projects.title: Make Your Own Property Trumps

materials.item: your results tables and bar charts from the experiments and the Property Ladder
8 stiff paper cards, the size of playing cards
pencils, a ruler and coloured pens
the materials from the experiments, for any new tests

projects.safety: Follow the safety notes of each test you repeat.

schedule.what: Choose 8 materials. Gather your results. Test any that are missing.
Turn your results into scores from 0 to 5. Make the cards.
Play your deck. Compare it with the rough deck and find where they differ.

projects.record: Eight cards, each with a material, a picture and five scores from 0 to 5. Plus a note on what surprised you.
projects.context: In this 3-day project you turn your own measurements into a card game. Each card has real scores for a material, from the tests you did. It is your own set of Property Trumps.

flow.do: 1. Gather your results from five tests. 2. The Property Ladder gives hard. 3. The droop test gives flexible. 4. The layers test gives transparent. 5. The vanishing drop gives absorbent. 6. The dry results of the Dry or Damp test give strong. 7. Choose 8 materials that appear in several tests. 8. Write their numbers in one big table, with a row for each material.
flow.say: You have done many tests. Let's collect the numbers in one big table. One row for each material, one column for each property.
flow.kid: Look at your results. Choose 8 materials. Put their numbers in one big table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Property Trumps project. You gather all your measurements into one table, one row for each material.
flow.parent: Not every material appears in every test. That is fine. This is the moment to fill the gaps by testing the missing ones, using the same method as before.

flow.do: Test any material that is missing a number. Use exactly the same method as before.
flow.say: Some boxes are empty. Let's fill them in with the same test, done the same way.
flow.kid: Fill the empty boxes by doing the same tests again.
flow.parent: If a test cannot be done, leave the box empty and give that card a 'no data' mark. Honest gaps are better than made-up numbers.

flow.do: 1. For each property, find the biggest number. 2. Give it a score of 5. 3. For every other material, work out its score: multiply its number by 5, then divide by the biggest number. 4. Round to the nearest whole number. 5. For absorbent, a short time is best. So multiply the shortest time by 5, and divide by each time.
flow.say: The best one in each test gets a 5. For the others, multiply by five and divide by the biggest. For example, say 2 cups when the biggest is 10. 2 times 5 is 10. 10 divided by 10 is 1.
flow.kid: The biggest number gets 5. For the others, multiply by 5. Then divide by the biggest. Round it.

check.q: In the droop test the most flexible strip dropped 10 centimetres. Another dropped 5. About what flexible score out of 5 should the second get?
check.why: 5 is half of 10. Half of 5 is 2 and a half. So the score is 2 or 3. Picking 5 gives everything a top score. Making scores this way means every test counts the same, with the best one always at 5.

flow.do: Make the cards. Write the material, draw a picture and write its five scores.
flow.say: Now make your cards. Each one has the material's name, a picture and five scores.
flow.kid: Make your cards. Write the name. Draw a picture. Write the scores.

flow.do: Play your deck like Property Trumps. Compare your card scores with the rough deck.
flow.say: Let's play with our own cards. Then compare them with the rough scores in the first deck.
flow.kid: Play your own cards. Then compare them with the first deck.

flow.do: Ask your child where their scores and the rough deck scores differ, and why.
flow.say: Where do your scores and the rough scores disagree? Which do you trust more, and why?
flow.kid: Where do your scores differ from the first deck? Which do you trust more?
flow.think: Your scores come from tests you did. Why can a test sometimes be more trusted than a guess?

challenges.title: The Mystery Material
challenges.problem: A grown-up has hidden three mystery samples in three numbered bags. You cannot look inside. For each one you have six tests. You must work out what it is like, and make your best guess about what it is.
constraints: You get only six tests for each sample.
You must write down every test before you do it.
You may not tear, cut or break the samples.
materials: three samples in paper bags, such as aluminium foil, waxed paper and a piece of thin plastic
a cup of water, a torch, a fridge magnet, a spoon, a small fork
general: Feel it, bend it, tap it, and see if it floats in water.
Hold it up to the torch to see whether it is transparent, translucent or opaque.
Drip a drop of water on it, to see whether it is waterproof.
Hold it against a fridge magnet. Scratch it gently with a fingernail.
creative: Warm a corner of it between your fingers for ten seconds. Does it soften, or does it stay the same?
Crumple it near your ear, and listen. Papers, foils and plastics each make their own crackle.
Rub it between your fingers. Does it feel cold, waxy or papery?
challenges.your_turn: Now be the one who hides the samples. Choose three, put them in bags, and write clue cards that name properties but not the material. Can your family guess?

flow.do: 1. Give your child the three bags. 2. Explain the rules: six tests for each sample, written down before testing.
flow.say: Each bag holds a mystery material. You can do six tests on each. Choose the tests carefully. Write each one down first.
flow.kid: Three bags hold three mystery materials. You may do six tests on each. Write each test down first.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Mystery Material. It is a detective challenge. You use property tests to work out what hidden materials are like.

flow.do: Help your child write a list of six tests that tell the most. Then do the same for the other two bags.
flow.say: Which six tests will tell you the most? Pick tests that split materials into different groups.
flow.kid: Choose six tests. Make them ones that tell you the most.

good: We only have six.
Some tests tell more than others.
A test that most materials pass tells us little.

flow.do: Do the tests. Write down the result of each in a table. After the last test, write your best guess for each bag.
flow.say: Do the tests. Write down every result. Then write your guess for what each sample is.
flow.kid: Do your tests. Write every result. Then write your best guess.
flow.parent: Good answers: bag 1 is shiny, flexible, opaque, waterproof and not attracted by the magnet, so it might be foil. Bag 2 is translucent, feels waxy and bends, so it might be waxed paper. Bag 3 is clear or cloudy, flexible and stretchy, so it might be thin plastic.

flow.do: Reveal what is in the bags. Ask which test gave the most useful clue.
flow.say: Open the bags. Were you right? Which test told you the most?
flow.kid: Open the bags. Were you right? Which test was the most helpful?
flow.think: Could two different materials give the same results on all six tests? What would you do then?
