challenges.title: The Privacy Window
challenges.problem: Your window faces a busy lane. You want sunlight to come in, but you do not want people in the lane to see inside. Use things you find at home to make a model window cover that does both.
constraints: Most of the light must still come through.
A person standing on the other side must not be seen clearly.
You can only use materials from home.
You must test your cover, not guess.
materials: a cardboard frame with a square hole about 20 centimetres wide, as a model window
butter paper, tissue paper, thin cotton, a plastic sheet, newspaper, a sheet of foil
scissors, sticky tape, a torch, a pencil
a friend to stand on the other side
general: Stick butter paper or tracing paper over the hole. It is translucent, so it lets in light but blurs the picture.
Layer thin tissue paper, a sheet at a time, until the person is just a shape.
Hang a net or a thin cotton curtain over the window.
creative: Cut a pattern of small holes, like an Indian jaali screen. Light and air come through, but eyes cannot see a clear picture.
Make a bamboo blind, with thin slats close together. Many Indian homes call these chik blinds.
Hang a khus tatti, a mat of woven grass. In summer, people sprinkle it with water, and it cools the air that comes through.
Stick thin coloured tissue paper in a pattern, like stained glass, and see what the light does.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own cover. Draw it, make it and test it. How much light did it let in? How well did it hide the person?

flow.do: 1. Make the cardboard frame with a square hole. 2. Ask your friend to stand on the other side and hold up a picture or a face. 3. Look through the empty frame. Everything is clear.
flow.say: This is our window. Look through the empty frame. You can see everything. How can we hide the person but keep the light?
flow.kid: This is your model window. Look through it. You can see everything. How can you hide the person and keep the light?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Privacy Window. It is a design challenge. You find a material that lets light in but hides what is behind it.

flow.do: 1. Try covering the hole with one material at a time. 2. Shine the torch from behind, and look from the front. 3. Write down: how much light? How clear is the person?
flow.say: Try each material over the hole. Ask two things each time. How much light comes in? How clearly can I see the person?
flow.kid: Cover the hole with each material. Ask: how much light? How clear is the person?
flow.parent: Good results: butter paper and thin cotton make a translucent window. Foil is opaque. A clear plastic sheet is transparent and hides nothing.

flow.do: Combine ideas. Try layers of tissue. Try a jaali pattern. Try two materials together.
flow.say: Can you combine two ideas? One layer of butter paper with a pattern of small holes? Test it.
flow.kid: Try layers. Try a jaali pattern. Try two ideas together. Test each.

ask.q: What happened when you added more layers?
good: It let in less light.
The person was harder to see.
There is a balance: enough layers to hide, not so many that it goes dark.

flow.do: Choose the best cover. Say why it works, using the words transparent, translucent and opaque.
flow.say: Which cover is best? Tell me why, using our three light words.
flow.kid: Which cover works best? Say why, using transparent, translucent and opaque.
flow.think: Old houses in India used jaali screens and khus tatti. What problems did they solve at the same time?

quiz.p: Which of these is a property of a material?
quiz.why: A property tells what a material is like, and waterproof does that. A spoon is an object. A kitchen and a shop are places. Picking 'a spoon' mixes up the object with the material it is made of.

quiz.p: A steel spoon and a steel tumbler are different objects. What is the same about them?
quiz.why: Both are steel, so both are hard, shiny and cold to touch. Picking shape, use or size mixes up the object and the material. Those are properties of the object, not of the steel.

quiz.p: A fingernail scratches chalk. A steel nail scratches a fingernail. Which is hardest?
quiz.why: If A scratches B, then A is harder than B. The nail scratches the fingernail, and the fingernail scratches the chalk. So the nail is hardest and the chalk is softest. Picking the chalk reverses the clue.
quiz.context: This is the scratch test. If one thing can scratch another, the first is harder.

quiz.p: Strip A drooped 2 centimetres in the droop test. Strip B drooped 9 centimetres. Which is more flexible?
quiz.why: A big drop means the strip bent a lot, so B is more flexible. A drooped only a little, so it is more rigid. Picking A is the common mistake of thinking a smaller number means more flexible.

quiz.p: In the dry or damp test, a dry toilet paper strip held 2 cups of water and a dry newspaper strip held 6. How many times as much did the newspaper hold?
quiz.why: 6 divided by 2 is 3. So the newspaper held 3 times as much. 'How many times as much' asks how many 2s make 6. 2 + 2 + 2 = 6, so the answer is 3. Picking 2 times or 4 times is a guess without working it out.

quiz.p: Glass is the right material for a window and the wrong one for a bridge. Why?
opts: The job decides which properties matter
Bridges are not made of anything
quiz.why: A window needs to be transparent. A bridge needs to be strong. Glass is transparent but brittle. No property is good or bad by itself. Picking 'glass is a bad material' misses that glass is perfect for its own job.

quiz.p: In the story, cotton thread held 14 shells in the damp dawn and 11 at noon. What did Shefali find out?
opts: Cotton thread is stronger when it is damp
The shells were heavier at noon
quiz.why: She kept the thread, the length and the shells the same. Only the dampness changed. A noon thread made damp held 14. So damp makes cotton a little stronger. 'Angry river' and 'tired thread' are guesses with no test behind them.
quiz.context: In The Thread That Held at Dawn, a girl dropped cowrie shells into a cup hung from threads, at dawn and at noon.

quiz.p: A glass bangle is hard to scratch but breaks when dropped. It is…
quiz.why: Hard is about scratching. Brittle is about snapping. Glass is both hard and brittle. Picking 'strong' mixes up hard and strong.

quiz.p: A paper clip stays bent. A plastic ruler springs back. A dry spaghetti stick snaps. Which one is brittle?
quiz.why: Brittle means it snaps or shatters instead of bending. The spaghetti snaps. The paper clip bends but stays bent, and the ruler springs back, which is called elastic. Picking the paper clip mixes up 'bends and stays bent' with 'breaks'.

quiz.p: A drop on paper towel vanished in 2 seconds. A drop on a plastic bag was still there after 2 minutes. What does this show about the bag?
quiz.why: A drop that stays on top means the water cannot get in. That is waterproof. Picking 'very absorbent' reads the result backwards. Picking 'the test did not work' is a common reaction to a zero. But a drop that stays is a real answer.

quiz.p: Diamond and pencil lead are both made of carbon. Why is diamond so much harder?
opts: The atoms are joined in a different pattern
quiz.why: The pattern of joins decides the property. In diamond every atom is locked to four neighbours. In graphite the atoms are in flat sheets that slide. Picking 'bigger atoms' is a natural guess, but the atoms are the same.

quiz.p: One sheet of butter paper is translucent. A tall stack of butter paper is opaque. What does this show?
opts: A property can change with thickness
Translucent and opaque mean the same
quiz.why: Each layer scatters and soaks up some light. With more layers, less comes through. So thickness changes the property. Picking 'two materials' is not true, because it is the same paper.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still not fully understand?
opts: What exactly glass is, and why a liquid turns into glass
That a steel nail is harder than chalk
That wet cotton is stronger than dry
quiz.why: Glass is an open puzzle. Its atoms are jumbled like a liquid's but stuck like a solid's. A famous physicist called it one of the deepest unsolved problems of solid matter. The other three have been tested again and again.

quiz.p: Toilet paper falls apart when it gets wet. Is that always a bad property?
opts: No, it depends on the job
Yes, because paper should be strong
No, because toilet paper is not a material
quiz.why: Toilet paper that falls apart in water does not block the pipes, so for its job that is useful. Weak is only bad when the job needs strong. Picking 'always bad' treats a property as good or bad on its own.

quiz.p: A steel spoon feels colder than a wooden spoon in the same room. What is the best explanation?
opts: Steel takes heat from your hand faster
quiz.why: Both are at room temperature. Your skin feels how fast heat leaves your hand, and steel pulls it away faster. Picking 'steel is a lower temperature' is the common idea. A thermometer would show the same number for both.

applications: Kitchens use steel for pans, because steel carries heat. They use wood or plastic for handles, which do not.
Raincoats and umbrellas are plastic or coated cloth, because they must be waterproof.
Towels and dishcloths are cotton, because cotton is absorbent.
Windows are glass, because glass is transparent. Bathroom windows are frosted, because translucent glass lets in light but hides us.
Bridges and railway lines use steel, because steel is both strong and hard.
Cricket bats are made of willow wood, which is strong but a little springy and does not split.
Wires are copper or aluminium, because metals carry electricity and heat well. Their covering is plastic, which does not.
Jewellers use a heat probe to tell a diamond from glass, because a diamond carries heat much faster.
Builders in hot, dry places make thick walls of clay or stone. Heat takes many hours to pass through them, so rooms stay cool in the day.
Engineers choose bamboo for scaffolding in India because it is strong and flexible and cheap.
Mattresses and pillows use foam or cotton, because soft, springy materials are comfortable.
Safety helmets and shoes use hard shells and soft padding, because each material does a different job.
Geologists test rocks with a scratch test and a hand lens. They use the Mohs scale in the field.
Space agencies, including ISRO, choose materials for rockets and landers that stay strong in heat, cold and vibration.
Doctors use materials in the body, like steel and plastic joints and dental fillings. These must be strong, safe and not rust.

open_questions.q: What exactly is glass? Is it a solid, a very slow liquid, or something else?
open_questions.why_open: Glass has atoms jumbled like a liquid's but stuck in place like a solid's. In 1995 the physicist Philip Anderson wrote that glass may be the deepest unsolved problem in solid physics. Scientists still argue about why a liquid turns into glass when it cools. One old idea is wrong, though: glass does not slowly flow at room temperature. Old windows that are thicker at the bottom were made that way.

open_questions.q: Can we work out a material's properties before we make it?
open_questions.why_open: In 2023, a computer program from Google DeepMind predicted 2.2 million new crystals, and 380,000 looked stable. Some chemists said many were not really new or useful. Nobody knows yet how many will turn out to be good materials.

open_questions.q: Is there a material harder than diamond?
open_questions.why_open: Computer models say a rare form of diamond with a different atom pattern, called lonsdaleite, could be harder. It is named after Kathleen Lonsdale. In 2014 other scientists said that natural samples are not a separate material. Whether a pure one can be made is still argued.

open_questions.q: How does a spider spin silk so tough, from water and a fly's meal, at room temperature?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have copied the chemical recipe. But nobody has made fibre as good as the real thing in large amounts without a spider.

open_questions.q: What is the strongest material that can possibly exist?
open_questions.why_open: Graphene is the strongest ever measured. A computer model says nuclear pasta, inside a neutron star, could be far stronger. Nobody knows whether anything stronger could exist, or could ever be made.

open_questions.q: Can we make materials that mend themselves, like skin?
open_questions.why_open: Some plastics and concretes in laboratories can close small cracks. None yet matches living things, which heal again and again for decades.

open_questions.q: Why is hardness so hard to define?
open_questions.why_open: Scratching, denting and bouncing back are different tests, and they do not always give the same order. Scientists use several hardness scales. There is still no single number that means 'hard'.

open_questions.q: What properties are there that we have not yet thought to test?
open_questions.why_open: Strength, hardness and shine were noticed long ago. Others, like how a material behaves at one atom thick, were only found when new tools arrived. We cannot know what we have not yet looked for.

maths.problem: In the droop test, a thin card strip dropped 3 centimetres. A paper strip dropped 9 centimetres. How many times as far did the paper drop?
maths.explain: The card dropped 3 centimetres and the paper dropped 9. 9 divided by 3 is 3. So the paper dropped 3 times as far. You can check: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9.
maths.context: The droop test measures how flexible a strip is. You let 10 centimetres of a strip stick out over a table edge, and measure how far its tip drops. A bigger drop means a more flexible strip.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how far each strip dropped
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show how the problem works.

maths.why_maths: Scientists do not just say 'the paper is more flexible'. They ask 'how many times as far did it bend?' Dividing one number by the other gives the answer.

maths.problem: In the vanishing drop test, one drop took 2 seconds on paper towel and 6 on cotton cloth. It took 25 on newspaper and 70 on printer paper. Draw a bar chart. Then say which surface is the third most absorbent.
maths.answer: Newspaper is the third most absorbent. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each, as tall as its number of seconds. A shorter time means a more absorbent surface. Put the times in order, from shortest to longest: 2, 6, 25, 70. The shortest is the paper towel. The next is the cotton. The third is the newspaper, at 25 seconds.
maths.context: In the vanishing drop test, you put one drop of water on a surface. You time how long it takes to vanish. A short time means the surface soaks up water fast.

answer_chart.title: Seconds for one drop to vanish
answer_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show how the problem works.

maths.why_maths: A bar chart turns a list of times into a picture. The shortest bar shows the most absorbent surface at a glance, and the order shows the ladder.

maths.problem: In the dry or damp test, a dry newspaper strip held 8 cups of water. A damp strip of the same newspaper held only 1 cup. Is 1 cup more or less than a quarter of 8 cups?
maths.answer: Less than a quarter. A quarter of 8 cups is 2 cups, and the damp strip held only 1.
maths.explain: A quarter of 8 is 8 divided by 4, which is 2. You can check: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8. The damp strip held 1 cup, which is less than 2. In fact 1 cup is half of a quarter, or one eighth, of 8 cups. So the damp strip held 7 cups fewer than the dry strip.
maths.context: In the dry or damp test, you hang a bag from a strip and pour in water, one cup at a time, until it tears. You do it with a dry strip and a damp strip. This shows if water changes how strong the paper is.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'less than a quarter as strong' tells us how much water changed the paper. Finding a quarter is the maths that turns 'weaker' into a number.

maths.problem: Aarav tested 12 things in the Kitchen Float Lab. 7 floated. How many sank? Of the 7 that floated, 3 were wooden. How many floaters were not wooden?
maths.answer: 5 sank, and 4 floaters were not wooden.
maths.explain: 12 things in all, and 7 floated. 12 take away 7 leaves 5 that sank. Of the 7 floaters, 3 were wooden. 7 take away 3 leaves 4 floaters that were not wooden. You can check: 7 + 5 = 12, and 3 + 4 = 7.
maths.context: In the Kitchen Float Lab, you guess whether things will float or sink in water, and then test them. You count how many floated and how many sank.
maths.why_maths: Counting how many things fall in each group is how a scientist spots a pattern. Here it shows that wood is not the only thing that floats.

maths.problem: Look at the ruler in the picture. It shows how far a paper strip dropped in the droop test. Each small mark is one centimetre. What is the reading?
maths.explain: The tip of the strip reaches the mark after 6 and before 8. It sits on the mark between them, which is 7. So the strip dropped 7 centimetres.
maths.context: In the droop test, you hold a ruler upright beside the table edge. You read how far the tip of a strip has dropped.

chart.title: A ruler, reading the drop of a paper strip in centimetres (cm)
chart.label: Each small mark is one centimetre.

maths.why_maths: A measuring tool only helps if you can read it. Reading the mark where the tip touches turns the picture into a number you can compare.

maths.problem: In the Property Trumps project, the most flexible strip dropped 10 centimetres. The paper strip dropped 8 centimetres. The best one gets a score of 5. What flexible score out of 5 does the paper get?
maths.explain: Multiply the paper's drop by 5. 8 times 5 is 40. Then divide by the biggest drop: 40 divided by 10 is 4. So the paper scores 4 out of 5. You can check: 10 times 5 ÷ 10 is 5 for the best strip.
maths.context: In the Property Trumps project, you turn your measurements into scores from 0 to 5. Then different tests can be compared on the same card.
maths.why_maths: A drop in centimetres and a time in seconds cannot be compared directly. Turning each into a score out of 5 puts them on one scale.

roots.context: We have been testing what materials are like, and found that some properties change with water and heat. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A dry strip of toilet paper can hold up a bag with water in it. Wet its middle with a fingertip, and the same strip tears with almost no water in the bag. Damp cotton thread holds as much, or a little more. So to know whether paper or thread will hold, you must also know whether it will get wet.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'paper is strong enough' or 'cotton is strong' as if strength were part of the material's name. But the same strip goes from strong to weak with a few drops of water, so a property needs a 'when' and a 'where'.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Dry or Damp test, a dry toilet paper strip held a bag with one or more cups of water, and a damp one tore with almost none. Cotton thread held about as much, or a little more, when damp. In the story, threads held more shells in the damp dawn than at dry noon.

three.who_am_i: Your body is made of materials too. Your skin stretches easily when it is damp, and can crack when it is very dry.
three.what_is_life: Life makes its own materials. Your body grows bone, hair and the clear lens of your eye, and mends them.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of materials whose properties change with heat, cold and water. A path that is firm today can be mud after rain.

roots.thread: One source shows up as everything there is. In materials you can see a small part of how this works. Diamond and pencil lead are both only carbon atoms, joined in two different patterns. Paper and cotton thread are both made mostly of cellulose, the substance of plant fibres. Yet water weakens paper and not thread, because their fibres are held together in different ways. The many materials around us are a few kinds of atom, arranged and joined in many ways.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka gives his son Shvetaketu a lump of salt and tells him to put it in water. In the morning the salt cannot be seen. But when Shvetaketu tastes the water from the top, the middle or the bottom, it is salty everywhere. Uddalaka says the finest part of everything is like this: unseen, yet everywhere.
teachings.link: You cannot see the atoms in a steel spoon or a strip of paper. But every property you tested, hard, shiny or strong, comes from them and how they are joined.

teachings.teaching: Nagarjuna, a Buddhist teacher of about the 2nd century CE, taught that nothing exists all alone. Everything is what it is because of other things.
teachings.link: The strength you measured depended on other things: the thread on the damp air, the paper on whether it was dry. Hard means harder than something else.

teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper and you see a cloud in it. Without the cloud there would be no rain, no tree and no paper. Thich Nhat Hanh called this interbeing.
teachings.link: Paper is made from wood fibres mixed with water, then pressed and dried. Water helps make paper, and in the Dry or Damp test water also took it apart.

science.text: Every property of a material comes from the atoms it has and how they are joined. Diamond and pencil lead are both only carbon.

Paper is made of plant fibres that stick to each other where they touch. Water gets between the fibres and loosens these joins, so wet paper tears easily. Makers add special chemicals to kitchen towels so that they stay strong when wet.
Philosophers still argue whether a stone is hard when nobody is testing it. Some say it has the property all by itself. Others say it only has the power to show it when it meets something.

other_view.who: Madhva, a philosopher of the Dvaita school in India about 700 years ago, and many scientists
other_view.view: The differences between things are real and lasting. A stone is hard in itself, even in a dark cupboard. Paper and cotton are two different things, even though both are made of the same plant fibre. In this view, the world is many real things, not one source showing up in many shapes.

how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years, people thought a diamond could never be destroyed. Its old Greek name, adamas, means 'unconquerable'. Nobody thought it had anything to do with black charcoal or pencil lead. In 1772 the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier heated a diamond with sunlight, focused by a giant lens. The diamond burned away. It made the same gas that burning charcoal makes, which we now call carbon dioxide. In 1797 the English chemist Smithson Tennant went further. He burned diamond and charcoal of the same weight. Both made the same amount of that gas. So a diamond is pure carbon, just like charcoal. But then why is one clear and hard, and the other black and soft? In 1913 William Henry Bragg and his son William Lawrence Bragg shone X-rays through a diamond. The pattern showed each carbon atom joined tightly to four neighbours. The atoms in diamond and pencil lead are the same. Only the way they are joined is different.
how_we_found_out.who: Antoine Lavoisier, Smithson Tennant, and William Henry Bragg with his son William Lawrence Bragg
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Diamond was thought to be a special stone that could never be destroyed, with nothing in common with black charcoal. Lavoisier and Tennant burned diamond and found it makes the same gas as charcoal, so it is carbon too.
